title: Oxtail Stew EVERYONE's Grandma Made (Why Yours Is GREASY)

scenes.text: Sweetheart, when I was a girl, oxtail was what the butcher practically gave away. Fifteen cents a pound in nineteen fifty-two. Nobody wanted those knobby bones with a little meat on them. Except my Grandma Pearl. She'd buy three pounds on Saturday, and on Sunday, the whole house smelled so good the neighbors found excuses to knock on our door.
scenes.caption: FIFTEEN CENTS A POUND

scenes.text: Today oxtail costs more than steak, and people tell me theirs came out tough, or swimming in grease, or the gravy tastes thin. So tonight I'm giving you Grandma Pearl's Sunday oxtail stew, every step, and the four mistakes that make it greasy and tough. And stay with me, because the last trick takes away all the grease, and it costs nothing but a night in the icebox.
scenes.caption: GREASY AND TOUGH

scenes.text: Grandma Pearl lived through the Depression on a farm outside Mansfield. She said nobody in her house ever threw away a single part of an animal. Oxtail, neck bones, shanks, the pieces the city people didn't want, were the best eating of all, if you knew how to cook them. And the secret, she said, was always the same. Time.
scenes.caption: THE SECRET WAS TIME

scenes.text: She'd put the pot on the back of her wood stove after church, and leave it there all afternoon while the family visited. By supper, the meat was falling off the bones, and the gravy was so rich and dark, it stuck to your lips. My father said it was the only food that made him forget his manners. He'd pick up the bones and suck them clean, and my mother let him.
scenes.caption: HE FORGOT HIS MANNERS

scenes.text: And oxtail isn't only a Grandma Pearl dish, honey. Jamaican families make it with butter beans and allspice. Korean families make a clear soup with it. Italians in Rome braise it with tomatoes and celery. Every kitchen in the world that ever had to stretch a dollar found oxtail. In a minute I'll tell you how to make yours go further, so three pounds feeds eight.
scenes.caption: EVERY KITCHEN FOUND IT

scenes.text: Here's what you need, honey. Three to four pounds of oxtail, cut in pieces. Ask the butcher for big pieces from the thick end if you can. Two onions, three carrots, and three ribs of celery, all chopped. Four cloves of garlic. Two tablespoons of tomato paste. Three cups of beef broth. One cup of red wine, or one more cup of broth. Two bay leaves, and a few sprigs of thyme.
scenes.caption: THE INGREDIENTS

scenes.text: And for the gravy, a quarter cup of flour for dusting the meat. Salt and pepper. And potatoes, either whole small ones in the pot, or mashed on the side. Grandma Pearl always made mashed potatoes, because she said a good gravy deserves somewhere to go. I've never found a reason to argue with that.
scenes.caption: SOMEWHERE TO GO

scenes.text: When you buy oxtail, honey, look for pieces with plenty of deep red meat around the bone, and a thin rim of white fat, not a thick one. The pieces from the wide end of the tail have the most meat. The little ones from the tip are mostly bone, but don't throw them out. They make the gravy rich. Ask the butcher for a mix of both.
scenes.caption: A MIX OF BOTH

scenes.text: Step one. Pat the oxtail very dry with paper towels. Season it well with salt and pepper on every side, then roll it lightly in the flour and shake off the extra. Mistake number one is skipping the drying. Wet meat steams in the pot. It turns gray instead of brown, and the stew never gets that deep, dark flavor.
scenes.caption: PAT IT DRY

scenes.text: Heat two tablespoons of oil in a big heavy pot, a Dutch oven, until it's very hot. Brown the oxtail a few pieces at a time, so they don't touch, about four minutes on each side, until they're dark brown all over. Don't crowd the pot. It takes about twenty minutes to brown them all, honey. It's the most important twenty minutes of the whole recipe.
scenes.caption: DON'T CROWD THE POT

scenes.text: Take the browned meat out and set it on a plate. Pour off all but two tablespoons of the fat. Then add the onions, carrots and celery, and cook them for eight minutes, scraping up all the brown bits on the bottom. Add the garlic and tomato paste, and stir for two minutes, until the paste turns dark red, almost brick colored.
scenes.caption: BRICK COLORED

scenes.text: If this is helping you, honey, tap the like button for me. It helps Grandma more than you know. Now pour in the wine, and let it bubble for two minutes, scraping the bottom. Add the broth, the bay leaves and the thyme. Put the oxtail back in, with any juice from the plate. The liquid should come about three quarters of the way up the meat, not cover it.
scenes.caption: THREE QUARTERS UP

scenes.text: Step two. Cover the pot and put it in the oven at three hundred degrees for three and a half to four hours. Mistake number two is rushing it. Oxtail is all bone, gristle and tough muscle. If you cook it for two hours, it's like chewing a shoe. At three and a half hours, all that gristle melts into the gravy, and the meat falls right off the bone.
scenes.query: Dutch oven in oven low heat
scenes.caption: THREE AND A HALF HOURS

scenes.text: And keep it low and gentle, sweetheart. Mistake number three is cooking it too hot, on a hard boil on the stove. Boiling makes the meat stringy and dry, even while it's sitting in liquid. The oven is better than the stovetop, because the heat comes from all sides, the way Grandma Pearl's wood stove did. Check it every hour, and add a little broth if it's getting low.
scenes.caption: LOW AND GENTLE

scenes.text: How do you know it's done? Take one piece out and poke the meat with a fork. If it slides off the bone with no pulling, it's done. If you have to tug, give it another thirty minutes. Pearl used to say, oxtail tells you when it's ready, honey. Your job is to listen.
scenes.caption: YOUR JOB IS TO LISTEN

scenes.text: So far, dry the meat and flour it, brown it dark in batches, cook the vegetables in the drippings, and braise it low in the oven for hours. Now the grease. Oxtail has a lot of fat, and it melts into the pot. And mistake number four is serving it right away, with a half inch of shiny grease floating on top. It coats your mouth and hides all the flavor.
scenes.caption: A HALF INCH OF GREASE

scenes.text: Here's the trick I promised, the one that costs nothing. Make it the day before. Let the pot cool, then put the whole thing in the icebox overnight. In the morning, all the fat will have risen to the top and turned hard and white, like a lid of candle wax. Just lift it off with a spoon, in big pieces, and throw it away. Every bit of grease, gone.
scenes.query: hardened fat lid on cold stew
scenes.caption: LIKE CANDLE WAX

scenes.text: And here's the best part. It tastes better the next day anyway. The gravy thickens up, the meat soaks up the flavor overnight. Pearl always made hers on Saturday for Sunday. On the day you serve it, heat it slowly on the stove, covered, for about thirty minutes, until it's bubbling and hot all the way through.
scenes.caption: BETTER THE NEXT DAY

scenes.text: And if you can't wait a day, honey, tilt the pot and spoon off as much fat as you can from the top. Then lay a paper towel flat on the surface for a second, and lift it off. It soaks up the last of the grease. Do it two or three times. It's not as clean as the icebox trick, but it works in a pinch.
scenes.caption: IN A PINCH

scenes.text: Before you serve it, take out the meat and keep it warm. Fish out the bay leaves and thyme stems. If the gravy is thin, simmer it on the stove for ten minutes, until it coats the back of a spoon. Taste it, and add salt and pepper. Pearl added a splash of vinegar at the end, just a teaspoon. It wakes the whole gravy up.
scenes.caption: IT WAKES IT UP

scenes.text: And here's how to make three pounds feed eight, like I promised. Pull all the meat off the bones, and stir it back into the gravy with a can of butter beans, or some egg noodles. Serve it over mashed potatoes or rice. Two pieces of oxtail on a plate feeds one person. The same meat pulled off the bones, with beans and potatoes, feeds two.
scenes.caption: THREE POUNDS FEEDS EIGHT

scenes.text: Oxtail stew keeps four days in the icebox, and it freezes for three months. Freeze it in the gravy, in containers with the meat off the bones, so it takes up less room. And save any leftover gravy. A spoon of it in a pot of soup, or over a hot biscuit on a cold morning, is a little bit of Sunday in the middle of the week.
scenes.caption: A LITTLE BIT OF SUNDAY

scenes.text: So one more time. Dry the meat, flour it, and brown it dark in batches. Cook the vegetables and tomato paste in the drippings. Wine and broth, three quarters up. Three and a half hours in a low oven. Make it the day before, and lift the fat off cold. A splash of vinegar in the gravy. That's Grandma Pearl's oxtail, and it's never greasy and never tough.
scenes.caption: NEVER GREASY

scenes.text: Tell me in the comments, sweetheart. Did your family eat oxtail when you were growing up? How did your grandmother make it? The whole playlist of Grandma's recipes is right there on your screen, and I'll see you in the next video. Good night, honey.
scenes.caption: HOW DID SHE MAKE IT?
